Sweetness
SWEET-nes
n.
From sweet + -ness. Renders the Hebrew māthōq, “sweet,” and the imagery of honey, the honeycomb, and the rock-of-honey throughout the Psalms; and the Greek glukuōs, “sweet.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Sweetness in Scripture is one of the most surprising and tender categories used for the Word of God, the LORD Himself, and the experiences of grace by the saint. The Psalmist’s great line sets the keynote: how sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth; and again: more to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb; and in the great Psalm 119: I have rejoiced in the way of thy testimonies, as much as in all riches. The Word is not merely true, not merely authoritative, not merely necessary—though it is all of these—but sweet, with the deep palatable sweetness that the saint comes to taste with an inward palate the natural man does not possess. Peter sets the same imagery at the start of the Christian life: as newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby: If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious. The taste of the LORD’s graciousness is the entry-point of the maturing Christian appetite. Psalm 34 makes the invitation universal: O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him. The category extends to the experiences of grace themselves: the sweetness of answered prayer, the sweetness of pardoned sin, the sweetness of communion with God in the closet, the sweetness of the Lord’s Supper, the sweetness of the gathered saints in worship. Even tribulation, says the Puritan tradition rightly tracing the biblical pattern, has its sweetness for the saint who has tasted the LORD’s comforts in it: it is good for me that I have been afflicted; that I might learn thy statutes. The pastoral application is double. First, the saint is invited to taste—to come to the Word, the LORD, the sacraments, the means of grace with an expectant inward palate and to develop the capacity to taste their sweetness. Second, the absence of any sense of sweetness in the things of God is the most ominous spiritual diagnostic Scripture supplies: the soul that has lost the sweetness of the Word is in danger; the soul that has never had it has not yet tasted that the Lord is gracious; and the soul awakened to the sweetness is the soul that has begun to live the regenerate life as God means it to be lived.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SWEETNESS as the quality of being sweet, in any of its senses; pleasing taste; agreeableness; melody; figuratively, gentleness; mildness; amiableness; in scripture, the deep palatable sweetness of God’s Word and presence to the regenerate soul.

expand to see more

SWEETNESS, n. — 1. The quality of being sweet, in any of its senses; as, the sweetness of fruit; the sweetness of perfumes. 2. Agreeableness of taste; that taste which gives pleasure. 3. Agreeableness; pleasing quality; as, the sweetness of disposition or temper. 4. Melody; pleasing harmony; as, the sweetness of music. 5. In scripture, the deep palatable sweetness of God’s Word and presence to the regenerate soul (Psa 19:10; 119:103).

📖 Key Scripture

Psalm 119:103 — "How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!"

Psalm 19:10 — "More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb."

Psalm 34:8 — "O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him."

1 Peter 2:2-3 — "As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby: If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The sweetness of God’s Word and presence is corrupted by the dry, dutiful register of the believer who reads Scripture as obligation without any expectation of tasted sweetness—and by the inverse mistake of seeking subjective emotional sweetness in worship and prayer apart from the substantive Word and presence that alone produce the biblical kind.

expand to see more

The dry, dutiful register is the most common contemporary corruption of biblical sweetness. The believer reads his Scripture as obligation, attends his services as discipline, prays his prayers as duty, all without any expectation that the Word will be sweet to his taste, that the LORD’s graciousness will be a tasted reality, or that the means of grace will produce in him the deep palatable enjoyment Scripture describes. The Psalmist who said how sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth would not recognize the inward palate of the contemporary dutiful believer, who has the doctrine of the Word’s authority but has lost the experience of its sweetness. Recover the doctrine and the expectation, and the appetite revives: come to Scripture with the inward palate ready to taste, ask the LORD to set the sweetness of His Word upon the soul, return to the texts that have once tasted sweet, and watch the inward palate awaken to the food God has prepared for it.

The opposite corruption is the seeking of subjective emotional sweetness in worship and prayer apart from the substantive Word and presence that alone produce the biblical kind. The believer chases the feeling-of-sweetness through music, atmosphere, and engineered experience, and identifies the engineered lift with the biblical sweetness that is in fact wrought by the gospel itself. The two are not the same. Biblical sweetness is the inward palate’s response to the actual substance of God’s Word and presence; engineered emotional lift is a separate thing that may accompany worship but is not itself the sweetness of which Scripture speaks. Recover both ends: come to the Word and the LORD expecting tasted sweetness as a real, experiential reality (against the dry corruption), and seek that sweetness in the actual substance of the Word and presence and not in engineered feeling (against the inverse corruption). The inward palate is real; the food is real; the sweetness is real; the believer’s discipline is to come to the table where it is served.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew māthōq (sweet) and the imagery of honey, honeycomb, and the rock-of-honey throughout the Psalms; Greek glukuōs (sweet)—the deep palatable sweetness of God’s Word and presence to the regenerate inward palate.

expand to see more

Hebrew māthōq (H4966) — sweet, pleasant (Prov 16:24; 24:13; Eccl 11:7; Ezek 3:3).

Hebrew māthaōq (H4985) — to be sweet, become sweet.

Hebrew d’vāsh (H1706) — honey (the sweetness comparison standard).

Greek glukuōs (G1099) — sweet (Rev 10:9-10, the bitter-sweet scroll).

Usage

"How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!—the inward palate’s response to the substance of God’s Word."

"O taste and see that the LORD is good—the LORD’s graciousness is itself a tasted reality, not merely an inferred one."

"Dry duty has lost the sweetness; engineered emotionalism substitutes a different feeling for it; biblical sweetness is the inward palate’s real response to real substance."
